shortcut_name: basis vectors imply a weighted tree
evidence: The surviving solution builds an adjacency list and uses a subtree DP: "dp[u] = minimum cost to connect all priority nodes in subtree of u". It relies on the input graph being a tree.
affordance_in_statement: The catalog of m vectors forms a basis for the subspace of all vectors in R^n whose coordinates sum to zero; m = n − 1.
removal_suggestion: Remove the guarantee that the m incidence vectors form a basis, while retaining the same objective and input format, so the catalog may contain cycles and the problem is no longer reducible to selecting the unique union of tree paths.

survivor_shortcuts.shortcut: Recognizes that the basis condition with m = n − 1 makes the underlying undirected catalog a tree, then sums exactly the edges needed to connect the priority vertices using subtree DP.
survivor_shortcuts.affordance: The catalog of m vectors forms a basis ... and m = n − 1.

common_affordance: The basis condition and m = n − 1 force the catalog graph to be a tree, making the required subset the unique minimal subtree spanning the priority vertices.

defeated_student_causes.why_failed: Its rooted DP reasoning appears to charge edges merely because a rooted subtree contains a priority vertex, without correctly checking whether that edge lies on a path between two priority vertices; this can include an unnecessary edge above the priority-containing subtree.

It uses a weight-sorted Union-Find/Kruskal-style approach. Kruskal can add cheap dangling edges that do not belong to the minimal priority-spanning subtree before all priority vertices become connected, so it does not solve the required Steiner subtree even on the given tree.

The shown approach treats the catalog as a generic weighted graph and does not exploit the forced-tree characterization correctly, so its selected connected structure is not guaranteed to be exactly the union of paths between priority vertices.

recommended_edit: Replace the explicit basis guarantee with arbitrary catalog vectors/edges, allowing cycles while preserving the same purchase-and-span objective; this removes the tree shortcut and forces a genuine minimum connected-subgraph/Steiner-style solution.
